sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: This is Mary Moore from the library of Congress. I will be interviewing Peter Kniskern at his home on -- at 3 -- 3175 Summit Square Drive, Apartment E7. It is July 16th, 2004. Chris Prusen (ph), from the Library of Congress is assisting me. And Peter has his friend, Yvonne Villar (ph), with us while we're interviewing today. Mr. Kniskern, when were you born?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I was born in May 4th, 1929.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: And what's your current address?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: 3175 Summit Square Drive, in Oakton, Virginia.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: What branch of service did you serve in in the war?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Well, officially, as far as enlistment is concerned, it was the United States Marine Corps. But that was when I was 16 or 17. I don't remember exactly which one, which order it came under. I think it was possibly 16 with your father's signature, or whatever it is. In any event, I got in at the time that I was able to get in. But prior to that, when I was about 13 and living in North Africa, in Tunisia, North Africa, where we -- as you know, where the US troops and allied troops invaded during the North African campaign. I volunteered my services to the US Army Air Force as a civil -- well, as an interpreter, and as such, just to give me something, I guess, that's basically -- they had to give me some sort of a title. They named me a civil affairs officer.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I guess that was in order for me to wear the uniform that I was given, and also not to be, you know, mistaken for somebody who shouldn't be wearing the uniform. But it was a rather strange set of circumstances. Of course I wore a great big band on my arm saying US. And when I was -- when I was able to, sometimes, of course, as a young kid would, I would take the band off and pretend I was in the corps, or in the Air Force. It was a lot of fun, of course, at that time. But it was a typical child approach to Walter Mitty's ambitions and so forth. So that's what -- that's what happened. So I was part of the North African campaign as a civilian volunteer, but I was paid the basic wage of the level that I was given in order to represent the armed forces.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: And what amount was that?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Gee, I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: I can --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I guess -- I think it was around, what, $30.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Thirty or $35, something like that. But they had to do that in order to get it down on paper, in order to make it a valid expense.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: So it came out in that way. But it was a great -- it was a great experience at that time.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Mr. Kniskern, could you tell me where you were born?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Let's not be so formal. Say Peter.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay. I'll call you Peter. I just wanted to show respect.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Oh, that's okay. That's very nice.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: I like the name of Peter. That's a great name.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah, sure. On this rock, you shall build my church, I believe, that's what the good Lord said. Yeah, you had asked me some basic questions about the reasons why I had been exposed to this experience in my life. And --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: But first, Peter --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: But first --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- I want to make sure I get the information.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yes, yes. I was born in Hinsdale, Illinois.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: And where is Hinsdale?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Hinsdale is outside of Chicago, I would say in the suburb -- suburbian areas, which is a very -- I was amazed. I visited that place years after, and I believe I discovered that it was exactly the same as when I left it, at least the downtown area, of course. But it's a beautiful little suburb, very quiet, and very -- very middle western, you know, that kind of thing. And regretfully, my mother and father had -- there's no sense into going into their background, except that they were seeking a divorce at that time. Thus, my mother took my sister and myself to join her family in North Africa in Tunisia where the government had requested help from experts in the field of agronomy from all over the world. Because that country was starving to death. I mean, the people were starving to death in the early part of the '20s, I think, or late '15s, or whatever it was. So --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Could you explain what agronomy is?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Agronomists, in other words, they were experts in the field of food -- food generation and so forth to make the earth, which was basically arid, produce huge crops of wheat and barley, and also to be able to raise sheep.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: You know, sheep on that particular -- on particular properties like that.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Was your mother a US citizen, or was she --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Mother was originally French. Her father was military and judgeship in the -- in France, but back in the early '20s. And she came to the United States to study.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And thus she became an American citizen when she married my father.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Oh, that's right. That's right.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: But the interesting part about that -- that's the maternal side. The paternal side is extremely interesting here, because it does have something to do with our history in this country.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I'm referring to the relationship between Napoleon and Nicholas Mason, who was my great-great-grandfather, and he was the educon (ph) of Napoleon when he was sent in isolation after he was arrested and sent out of the country. And then subsequent to that, as you know, he escaped from the island of St. Helena, came back to the continent to try to take over the government again so that he would still be emperor, but he didn't succeed. And while he was doing this, my great-grandfather was still part of his, quote, unquote, administration. And then he realized it was a lost cause, so he left Napoleon and stayed in Paris. But he thought there might be some repercussions against his children, so he sent his children to the United States.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And his daughter, Pauline, married a Pollack, which is the line of my family. And she died in -- she died in 1884, I think, or whenever the heck it was, I think. But very, very, very old. She had lived many, many years. So that's the relationship between the two things. But again, coming back to Hinsdale, the separation occurred. We left -- and we left, and left the country, and brought my sister to a boarding school in Edinboro. And then my mother and I proceeded once I recuperated from a very bad case of pneumonia. Again, there's no sense into going into that. I almost died. But still, after this, we went further on our journey to France, and then from France, our objective was to go to Tunisia.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And very strange at that point, because transportation was limited. And so there were no cabins, no nothing. We had to take a pack boat. Pack boat. And we slept on the deck. I'm writing a book now which eventually will come out, but --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: And when -- you were approximately seven at this time, correct?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah, right. And some of the experiences on that boat were rather interesting, having to do with snakes and charmers that were aboard that boat and so forth. But I've got that in the --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Yeah, that's fine.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: -- in my report. But we -- our objective was to go to Tunisia and join my mother's brother, who had already been there for several years, had already started the program with the government on a quasi private basis in order to make the land produce. And that was the objective. So many, many people, many agronomists, shall we say, came from France, came from Borneo, Sumatra, England, America, et cetera, and settled into that concept of helping the Tunisians recoup, shall we say, their viability in an economic way. And that's when I -- and prior to that, as you know, the United States saved Tunisia from the barbary pirates. So that's -- as of that -- prior to that time is when Tunisia became a great admirer of and an ally of the United States and so forth. And that's why we were able to do certain things during World War II that normally would not have been able to be done.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: That -- that's the reason we came there. And I resided in that place for a good five, six, seven years.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And learned the language, of course, and learned French, learned the folk ways and the mores of the -- the various indigenous peoples. It's quite interesting. I was forbidden to play with the Arabs, because that's not something that the colonists allowed their children to do. So I had to find everything on my own. But I created -- I created an interesting life for myself. I would never regret that experience. It was very, very interesting.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Was it difficult --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And the war --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- leaving your father behind?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: At that age --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Yeah, you were --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: At that age, you don't really -- you don't really remember those things, but the one vivid thing I recollect is that in the -- in the station of Chicago, where we went to, you know, get the train, he brought us that far. Of course, it was a very, very bad day that day. It was very cold, it was snow, sleet.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Et cetera, et cetera. And he was wearing a very deep gray coat, and he would constantly hunch himself into that to protect himself. But when he was finally leaving the station from us, when it was time to go, I just remember a very vivid picture of his shrinking into that coat. And then that stayed in my mind for the rest of my life. Of course, it was because he was very sad. And regretfully, I never got to know my father very well. It was not -- because he was more of a -- you know, he was the worker. He was the one that punished and things like that. So you didn't get to know your father very well during those days, unless it was an extremely closely knit family. And we did not -- we did not have that. It was basically my mother. My mother was the one. So that's what took place.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay. Now, I would like you to tell me how you got into working with the Army and being an interpreter and translator. I mean, I read something that you were actually out looking for a job, and --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: What I said --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- and you wanted to get a job?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: What I wanted to do, I didn't just want to be sitting around doing nothing, and since I spoke the language, I thought I would offer my services to the thing -- to the Air Force. But what happened, is that we were really obliged to flee from our plantation --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Oh, yeah, because you were in Tunis at first.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: -- in Sidi Bou Said. No, Tunis is the capitol of Tunisia.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: We were in the far south.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: That's where you were living?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah, in the --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: From the time you were seven on?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: We were living in the Sahel. And the Sahel was a very dangerous place, because that's where a lot of the -- well --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: The attacks?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: A lot of the attacks, a lot of the local attacks from the infintatas (ph) -- infin -- infantatas. But, yeah, I'm talking about there were -- there were local people that were attacking us also.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Because they thought the Germans was going to win.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Oh, right, I see.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And then when the Germans lost, they came to the Americans, you know, and fawned all over them and all of that. But then we were obliged to realize that this was -- you know, that was the end. We had to get out. So we drove all the way from Tunisia to Algeria.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: That's how we got to Algeria. That's when I went around --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: That's when the event --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: -- to the Red Cross, to headquarters, Air Force, and I said, "Here's my American citizenship. I'm interested in doing this." And they hired me at 13. I was very, very surprised, but very happy, because I wanted to do something that was -- you know, that was beneficial and fun.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: And you wanted the chocolates.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I wanted the chocolates. I wanted all the goodies that the PX had available. Oh, boy, that was great.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Yeah, the newspaper articles I read said that you -- one of the benefits was you were able to eat with --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- with the --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: With the troops, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: With the troops.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. Not only that, but I wasn't restricted to eating with the troops. I could eat with the officers, too.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Right. Because you were a civilian.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: That was a -- that was a great advantage. I got to play both sides. So that was -- that's why I was able to do a lot of things that normally a kid at 13 would never even be -- think that he could do, you know. So that's --Oh, yeah, before leaving, there was a big, big battle that was fought on our plantation. And the outcome was that our tanks, which were the Sherman tanks were badly outgunned, outmaneuvered by the German Panzer tank and the Tiger tank. We had tanks all over the place that were blown up and so forth.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: It was -- it was really -- it was really bad the way our boys were destroyed by these people, because whenever -- whenever a tank of the enemy would hone in on one of our tanks, and they would shoot for the turret of the tank, because they knew that we stored our ammunition in the turret of the tank. So all they had to have was one straight shot into the turret, and it would ricochet inside and blow up the whole thing and kill everybody, of course. So they used me also at that time to go and locate -- I don't want you to react -- but very, very bad things, you know, graves of boys that had been killed, and, geez, it was bad. And I saw things at 13 which naturally formed my mind for the rest of my life. I should have never seen those things.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: At that age?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Horrible.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Or any age.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: It was really horrible. And so our -- as I said, our plantation was the main battle, and we lost. And then we sent in some heavier tanks later on, and that's when there was the big battles of the Kasserine Pass, and the Faid Pass and all of that. And it was very interesting because from our home, which was really built on the site of a Roman city, dating back about 4,000 years, we were high enough to be able to see what was going on in the passes when the Germans were there. And also when the Americans were there. So when the Germans were there, we would bomb the living you know what out of them. And then, vice versa, Germans would come with the Messerschmitts and the Stukas and their bombers and bomb the heck out of us. So that was, again, an experience that, you know, you just never could fathom that that would happen in your life. But that -- I -- that really made me age pretty quickly.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh. What were your experiences with interpreting and translating?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: A lot of it had to do with assisting the officials trying to locate headquarters, residences, things of that kind. And --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: So did you --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Excuse me.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: I also know that you went with -- or you helped find apartments?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah, I helped them do that.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: So would you -- with your translating, would you have -- or interpreting, would the soldiers or officers be with you when you were --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- showing the apartments.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: And that's when you were doing the interpreting, or that's one way you did it?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Right, right, right. And -- and the other cases when they needed me, it had to do with certain things that were going on in the community so they could understand the community and what was going on. Merci.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Good idea. Yeah, having -- having some water helps when you're going to be talking for an hour or more. Thank you, Yvonne.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: The -- but as I said, there are a lot of things -- a lot of details which I'm probably forgetting. Oh, well, yeah, that is well known, of course. During the North African campaign, as you know, Field Marshal Rommel came in from the south and the Americans came in from the north so that there was a huge conflagration between the two forces at that time. And our -- our home probably was the only one that was not really bombed out or ransacked or something. The reason being that my stepfather was Swiss, and as Swiss people, we're not part of World War II, they were neutral. It was -- it was straight the one time, you know, that it was straight, and one of the -- two or three of the bullets came right above my sister's bed where her pillow was. Had she been in there, she would have been killed. But the -- those things just took place at that time. And we felt that while we were gone, that everything was going to be destroyed, but apparently it was not destroyed. And it was my understanding that since my father -- stepfather, rather, spoke fluent German and English and various other languages, that he had occasion to invest with Rommel, and I think Rommel visited our house. That was my understanding. Because let's face it, it would be the headquarters, shall we say, of the opposition, although it wasn't the opposition, it was the neutral ground. And that part was extremely -- it would have been extremely interesting, except we weren't there. We had already left. We had escaped. And one of the main reasons we escaped when we did is had my sister been there at the time the Germans got there, she would have been sent to Baden Baden, Germany, you know, where they sent all the women of nice families and so forth to basically reproduce for the Fuhrer. That's what it was all about.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Oh, yeah, that took place.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: But you got out --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: But we got out of there in time, yeah.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- before all of that. Now, your -- your mother was, I don't know if captured is the right word, but she was sent somewhere, I thought, or was she -- was she in -- did she go to Algeria with you?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: She went to Algeria with me.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Was there some point that she was taken or --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I think you may be referring to the visit which we had with the wife of the American consul general in Hammamet, which was a summer residence.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And I was invited to go there. And it was the lady in question, Mrs. Madge Springs, who was taken by the Germans and taken to Germany.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And apparently -- and she was a spitfire. I mean, really a spitfire. And she did so many things to get out of this, when she was taken to Germany, that they sent her back to England. The Germans got rid of her. They said, "We can't take her." Otherwise, they would have killed her. You know, the German officers were, you know, doing what the other people were doing, et cetera, et cetera. But it didn't work. She was scratching and spitting and -- oh, it was really quite a report on that.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: So after your --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: But I spent quite a bit of time with them there.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- after your home -- your home in Tunisia was attacked --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Right. The home wasn't attacked.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: The plantation was attacked.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: The plantation.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Sorry, yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: The plantation experienced the battles. But it was not with the idea of capturing the house.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Or the property. It was just because they encountered each other on the battlefield in that region.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And that's the plains of the Gamuta (ph), and that was very, very, very well known during that period of time.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: So after that attack happened, then your family moved to Algeria.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Well, my mother, my sister, and myself, a friend of ours, whose son and I were friends, and with whom I had gone to school, we drove. He -- he took the responsibility of driving us out there. And left my stepfather and my uncle, who were on the properties, to guard the properties and to protect. But we drove all the way to Algeria.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: And that's where you got the job?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: That's where I got the job.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: So tell me your experience from any -- any experiences that you had during that time when you were working any other experiences that you haven't talked about yet.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Well, one thing -- one thing, again -- again, being a free agent, shall we say.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: -- I would have access to command cars, transportation, anything that a civil affairs officer would be able to get. And I made friends with a lot of aviators. And I would pester them to death to take me up in their plane. And so one day, we -- one day, we drove -- well, the chauffeur drove me over to an air base, and during that time, there was an attack by the Germans. And this was at night, 7:00, 8:00 at night, after we had eaten, we heard the sirens and so forth. And, naturally, what does a kid do? He runs to the top of the building rather than to run down and hide in the cellar. And there was a pretty nasty -- nasty thing that happened on the roof. One of the -- one of the bombs did blow up and shrapnel came extremely close. In fact, it hit one of the helmets that I was wearing, one of the things. And after that -- and, of course, the commanding officer heard about it, and he said, "You're no longer to do this." So I got away with a lot of stuff, a lot of stuff. But finally, one of the guys, and God, he got killed later, he was nice, very nice guy, put me -- took out his radio in the back of the -- of the plane, and he stashed me in there. Literally stashed me, because that's no room for a human being. He stashed me in there, and sure enough, he took me up there. And he did all the loops, the loops, and all the this, and all the that. I got sick as a dog.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I said, "Take me down, take me down, I won't bother you anymore." Lo and behold, that's what happened. He took me down and said, "Now you are satisfied?" I said, "I won't ask you again, I swear, I swear." But then I found out later on in a -- he was killed in air action. So there was one of the things. I'm sure there are a lot of other things, but the trouble is you can't --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: You can't delve into that and remember. That sounds interesting.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: I was wondering what kinds of services they had you provide them when you were acting as their interpreter, what languages did they need you to speak for them, what exactly -- other than locating homes, and you needed to utilize things because you were --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Right, right.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- a native of the area, what were you --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Right. Right. For the most part, naturally, it was French, in as much as I had learned French fluently. And, of course, believe it or not, I was forced to go to a school which was 99.99 percent Arabic attendance, and I was forced to learn part of the Koran because that was part of the curriculum. So I had learned some Arabic, and so that was a dual language opportunity there. But for the most part, it was French, because Algiers, of course, was, you know, French oriented, shall we say. And they asked all sorts of questions in that language. So for the most part -- but there were occasions when a little bit of Arabic was used, but then as they say, when you never -- when you don't use a language, you'll lose it, especially at that stage of the game. Now, if I were put back into full emersion in a country without any kind of access to English or French or anything else, I would learn Arabic pretty fast.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: How much do you use the two languages now, French and --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I use -- I use French and Spanish now more than I did before, which was French and Arabic. But my French permitted me to learn Spanish, and I really got Spanish down.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Oh, so now you know four languages?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Well, including English, I guess, yeah.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Right. Including English?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Tell me about your education, when you -- when you left United States, you were about seven, and so you were getting ready to start school, or maybe you had already --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- had school in the United States?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: And then about your education, when you went to Algeria, and you were --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Right, right.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- working with the Air Force?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Right. Well, as I mentioned, in the initial stages, I had to go to local school, local schools, and that's where I picked up the little Arabic that I knew later on. But then, as time went, I was sent to an institution outside of Tunis, which was a -- was a boarding school for boys only.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: So you were not living at home at that point?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I didn't live at home at that point. But prior to that, I was living at home.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And then I would ride -- I would go by horseback, I would go to school every day and then come back home, and it was a good 20 kilometers or so, you know.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: And when you were at boarding school --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Both ways.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- did you stay at, like, the school for a week and visit home on the weekend?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Oh, no, no, no, no. No, no, we just lived there, period.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: And --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: We just --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: But you were away from your family?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: From the family, oh, yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: But it wasn't that far from where your family was?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: From Tunis to where we were, to the plains of the Gamuta (ph) was pretty doggone far, yes.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: It was a good three hours or four hours of driving in the desert.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: But in those days, it was much more difficult --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- than what people would think nowadays?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Some very interesting experiences on the highways, which I'm referring to in the book and so on. But again, that would be more of a detailed report. But very funny.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay. Go ahead on with your education. You were at a boarding school.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Okay. Until 1939, and then 1939, of course, was when the war between the -- between Germany and France was declared, and so it was impossible to stay in Tunis. And so I had private tutoring by my mother, both in the languages and the whole thing. She was a great teacher. And she taught me also music and things of that kind.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I wish I had, you know, stayed into that, and I would have learned a lot more, but I didn't. But that -- that was the only way I could have any kind of a continued educational program, by having private tutoring. And then -- and then later on, of course, I was able to get into, again, another school, when it was safe to be away from home. And then I would live there as a boarding -- as a border, like all the boys did. Well, most of the boys did. But at that time, of course, this was not co-ed, this was strictly --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Strictly boys in the grow ups -- growing up stage. Oh, yeah. When I came back to the United States, of course --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: You were still young?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I was still young, yeah. I was about 14 at that time, 14 and a half, 15. And then I went to military school, Tennessee Military Institute. I was going to become an officer. I had gotten -- my aunt had gotten me an appointment to a -- not Annapolis, to West Point.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Trouble is, I didn't get back to the States in time to take advantage of it.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: So I missed out on that one. So I --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: When you were in Algeria and working with the Army and Air Force, were you at that time being tutored by your mother?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: No, I was being tutored by a special -- there was a special school in Algiers for foreigners.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And as a result, there was the continuity of my education. Of course, I -- it was not -- it was not unusual for me to skip classes to go to that famous airport where I wanted to go fly, but --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: You skipped out just to --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Not all -- not all the time. I skipped out. I skipped out, yeah, and, of course, my mother was told about it, and so I was told not to do it again. And, of course, I did it again and so on. But here's -- here's the thing. Here's the funny part. Here's the funny part. I really got into trouble. Let's see. How did that start out? Oh, yes. I was supposed to go visit part of the family which had escaped from Tunisia, and which had settled in the mountains of Algeria, and the place was called Kuvaney (ph). Kuvaney. And that was really the only place where you could be safe from the Germans at that time. You had to stay there. You had to stay in that -- in those mountains, otherwise you would be captured and whatever. But what I did is that when I left Algiers to go to Konay (ph), I said, "Huh, I'm going to be a smart one." And what did I do? I took off --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Your band?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I took off my US band, and I traveled all the way to Setif. And Setif was where they had those horrible massacres between the Arabs and the French and so forth during that period of time. And the allied troops were there. And I was received very nicely, lots of candy, lots of chocolates, lots of goodies, lots of laughter and so forth and so on. And then the next day, I said, "I'm on my way to Setif. I need to get there and so forth." The next day a couple of guys came to get me and they said, "Well, we're really ready to go to Setif. You want to have a ride?" So they said we're going by train. And so I said, "Yeah, that sounds like fun." And just to -- just a kid's reaction. You know, all of this was so exciting, it was so new, it was so unusual. Lo and behold we got on the train, and, you know, everything was fine. We would sit and chat and eat and play, and one guy had a guitar, and we just had a great -- a great old time. I was just about to say a gay old time. We can't say that anymore. Anyhow, and then about a couple of hours later, I went into the hall, because in -- in France, I don't know if you know that -- well, I guess we do have that in our trains, too, they had a corridor.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Where you can go, and you can see outside besides --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: -- you know what you see inside. And then you got the private compartments where we were, and I wasn't paying attention. So I went out, and as a thirteen-year-old kid, I reasoned. I said, "Now, wait a minute, this train is going north. It's not going south." And I -- and I kept quiet. And I kept thinking, and I didn't know what to say. And lo and behold, later on, I said -- you know, I was very surprised. I went out in the corridor a while ago, and I said, "The train" -- "the train is going north. And guess what? The smoke is going south." No, I didn't say that. I said, "What's going on?" And then they broke down and told me, they said, "You're being arrested for a German spy. You're being arrested, and you are to arrive in Algiers. There will be an armed guard waiting for you, and you will be taken to headquarters." And, of course, I knew this was a big farce, so I laughed, and I laughed, and I laughed. And then it got to be worse. And then I got to worry, and, well, this isn't exactly the way it should be. And sure enough, we got to Algiers. We didn't get to Konay (ph). And there were four MPs with their Tommy guns came in to get me, took me out, took me to headquarters. I said, "You guys are absolutely nuts. I'm not a German spy. Captain Steward and Bill Motford will testify -- testify to this. And we went to look for Captain Bill Motford, who was the commanding officer of the 12th Air Force in the section where I was working. He's the one that gave me the job. And they tracked him down in Constantine. Constantine was a place way south. And they told him what they had told me. And all they could hear at the other end was the guy just rolling on the floor. He said, "He's not a spy. He's the guy that I hired," and so forth and so on and so forth. So what happened? So they let me go. But what they did, is they put me in a truck that was going to Constantine to join Captain Motford. That truck had gasoline, bedon (ph), in the back of it. And, of course, you know, those containers, you know, the big -- what did we call them? The jerry cans? Remember the jerry cans? Full of gasoline or milk or this and that. But those big, big -- those big jerry cans, you know. And, of course, the fumes overpowered everybody. I got sick as a dog, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. So we finally got to Constantine, and then they turned me over to two officers who took me under their wing and took me to their -- their place where they lived. And they said, "Well, Peter, what would you like to do tonight? We're going to go out and eat," and so forth. And, "There's a big officer's dance, would you like to go?" I said, "Oh, why not." He said, "Here, put on my" -- "put on my uniform and put on my cap." He was a lieutenant. And, of course, at that time, I looked very advanced for my age. And I -- you know, not having learned the hard way, I did it again. And I almost got caught, because as I went into the door, the two MPs that were guarding the door, they said -- the other one said, "Do you think that's possible? Do you think that's possible?" He goes, "I don't know," queech (ph). I just went in there, and I enjoyed it.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: That's --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: So that was a lot of fun. I never learned. I never learned. It was just a lot of fun. And then I was already 14, you know. But I looked about 16 or 17 type. And so I really did get away with murder. (End of Tape 1, Side A.) Yeah, there's something very interesting I would like to share with you. Still about the -- about the Tunisia experience. There was a story -- I wasn't there, thus, I cannot prove this. But I understand that it is genuine. Namely, prior to the invasion of North Africa -- and by the way, had we not invaded North Africa when we did, Russia was all set to send in paratroopers during the war. That's just a little bit of a tidbit there. But, anyhow, when -- prior to the invasion, the Germans occupied North Africa, and the Americans made a deal with the Vichy government, because the Vichy government was in power at that time, to turn their machine guns around when we invaded and shoot at the Germans rather than the Germans -- rather than shooting at us. And in order to do that, of course, that required quite a bit of gold to change hands. Now, what happened, is that there was a meeting that took place on one of the beaches of the North African coast between General Clark and General Mast, who was the commanding officer, shall we say, of the resistance troops in North Africa. And then -- there was another one. Pittman Springs, who was the counsel general of the United States in Tunis. So this must have been -- this must have happened on the coast in and around Tunis or further north, I'm not sure. But anyhow, what happened, is an US submarine deposited Mark Clark, Pittman Springs on the shore, and they met Mast on the coast. And they had a powwow you. Mark Clark came ashore with those fatigues. Remember the fatigues? The big ones with the big --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Kind of like what they wear nowadays?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah, with the big pockets on the right side.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: With the big pockets and stuff.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Ladened with gold.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: That must have been heavy.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Are we doing it? Yeah, we're doing it.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: That must have been heavy --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Ladened with gold.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- to carry around.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Extremely -- but he came from the submarine to land, right? Well, guess what happened? They sent messages back and forth from the beach to the submarine. The Germans intercepted the messages and sent the troops out from Tunis to capture those people that were out there, namely them. And thank God they were aware of the fact that the Germans had intercepted it. So everybody scrambled into the rubber boats to get back to the -- to the submarine, but the only one that didn't make it was Mark Clark. He hung onto the back of the rubber boat. And, of course, with the strength of the power of the boat, the rapidity of the current and so forth, it ripped -- it ripped the whole thing, including the gold, off of his body, and it sank. And to this day, we're not sure whether General Mast or some of the others that were there got that gold. But that was the gold that was going to pay the Vichy troops to fire on the Germans. That's a very interesting -- that's a very interesting story. Whether that's a tidbit, which it's true or not, I don't know. But they had to pay the troops one way or the other. And who was going to do that? Not Britain. The United States. And who had the gold? We did. And so who was going to transport the gold? The submarine. So that all tied in very, very neatly. That was another experience that -- that I experienced there. You might put that on mute for the moment. I thought -- I thought here might be interesting, for historical purposes, is that the United States did not just invade North Africa in one place, it invaded North Africa in several places along the northern coast of North Africa. That would be between Algiers and Gibraltar, if you went on a straight line. So several points of landings took place. And then the troops drove north -- drove south do meet up with General Patton's troops in the south. And then they formed a wedge. They formed a wedge against the Germans that had accumulated their troops by then, you see, because they had escaped from the North African desert and Libya and so forth. They had escaped that route. They had taken that route and came all the way into the Cap Bon area of North Africa. So we had to find a way whereby we could defeat the Germans and then push them out to sea. I think that that was the original objective. But we formed that wedge, it went down and met up with Patton, who fought -- whose people fought very valiantly in the Faid Pass battles, as well as the Kasserine Pass battles. Now, these are very well known in the annals of history, of course, of warfare, but not just in general. And it was extremely interesting to see what developed later on that there was a -- they also formed a pincer -- a pincer movement to catch the German Rommel's army, completely catch them and push them out to the sea. And this is exactly what took place at the time. But as I said, this would have been an extremely different story today had the United States not invaded North Africa when it did, because Russia, and this is -- this is on the reports and everything. Russia had intended to invade North Africa by air, not by sea. Had they done that, they would have formed beach heads and so forth. And the Americans would not have been able to come aboard because then there would have been, you know, that kind of a situation. There would have been a war. But a lot of things took place there that were extremely interesting. Had I been a little bit older, I would have understood them much more than I can today, which is normal.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Right. Right.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And that's why you have to try to delve into the past and bring out the details of some of these things. I'm sure I'm over looking a lot of things.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Well, when you were --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: But anyhow --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: When you were -- I think it was in 1943, that they decided to send you back to the United States because of the danger that -- how dangerous it was?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Well, in 1943, at that stage of the game, it's not a question too much of danger, it was a question that I was a young kid of 14 that needed to get back to studies. And then that's when my --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Right. That's true. Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: -- my great aunt got in touch with the Secretary of State, and all of that kind of stuff, and then they sent messages back and forth and so on, because my Great Aunt Katherine was very much the initiator. She's somewhat like you. She was very -- she was extremely innovative, she was extremely ahead of things. She was very determined to do something to save her nephew.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Well, that's a nice compliment --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: So that's normal.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- Yvonne?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah, it is, it's a very nice compliment to Yvonne, because that's what she is, too. She's very supportive, and she's extremely -- she's very much like that herself. That's why I wanted her to be part of this, because sure I went into some of these details in the past, as far as pictures are concerned, but she never heard the viva voce story. You know, she never heard the real thing the way it took place. And the steps, and so on. So I thought this was a nice opportunity to bring her into it.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Well, I want you -- unless you have anything else to share about when you were a civilian within the -- the Air Force Army --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Army Air Force.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- Army Air Force during World War II, that we move on.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: And if you tell me a little bit about your -- your trip home. And because I know you went from a couple of different places. You were -- I forget exactly where you went first, but I know --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: We were on vacation in Lasheeba (ph), where we had our summer home.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: With your family, with your mother?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Lasheeba (ph), yeah.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And it was decided at that point -- it really wasn't the military that decided I should come back.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: It was the family that decided that they wanted me to get back to my studies. Because I was supposedly preparing for a doctorship and so forth and so on. And if I didn't get my studies at the time, it would not happen and all that kind of stuff. But anyhow, the idea was let's send Peter back to his father, let him go to military school, let him regain the knowledge of America. I didn't know the language too well. I had forgotten my English. And that would be a good exposure for him, which I've always believed that that's a very good thing for young men. It does teach all sorts of things. And so that's -- that is what happened, you know, when I came back, I didn't just go to local school. Later on I did, but not at the beginning. I went to military school, learned the language. And I took an interest in Spanish, and that's where I started learning Spanish.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And that progressed and progressed and progressed and progressed because I visited South America and stayed there quite a while, and learned the language, and developed the language, which I'm using, as I said, on a daily basis here, so I get a chance to practice on a daily basis.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: So that's when I went to -- I went to that military school, and then I went to local school. And then it was time to look at the Marine Corps.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: So you served in the Marine Corps --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I volunteered.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- from very -- towards the end of World War II.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Towards the end of World War II, yeah.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: And --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I thought that it was all over in 1945.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Well, that's --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: But apparently for the ALMAR, and for the -- for the decorations and for the this and that and the other, it carries into 1946, and that is -- which is the official date, somewhere.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: The end?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Somewhere, I don't remember exactly where. But it carried into that. So I was fortunate -- I was fortunate enough not to get into battle. We were prepared for battle, so our outfit was designated as a recipient of certain awards and things like that, because we were going to go into Beirut. This was at the time when the Beirut problems took place back in the 1940 -- '47, I think. 1947.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: That would have been a very interesting thing, but I would have been in battle then.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Now, you volunteered, so you enlisted in the Marine Corps?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yes, I had to have my father's signature in order to --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Right. Were you living in Hinsdale?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: No, I was living in Kirkland, Ohio, at that time.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay. Okay. And why did you decide to join the Marine Corps?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Well, let's face it, you know, when a kid of 12 or 13 or 14 years of age gets used to doing what he wants to do --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Independent?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: -- pretty much -- and not being dependent on anybody, et cetera, comes into a melieu of discipline and having to be home by certain hours and things of that kind, you sort of say to yourself, that's not what I expected by coming back to the United States.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: So I knew that I could enlist in the Marine Corps, and then with my father's signature, I was able to enlist. And I think that that was probably the best for everybody around, because my father had remarried, thus there was a certain amount of tension between the --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh, having --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: -- the family, the kid from the previous marriage, et cetera, et cetera. And so forth, so forth. To I think this was a good thing for them, and it was a good thing for me. Because first of all, it made me physically. It really built me physically.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Um --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Something I hadn't had for a while.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Yeah, I'm going to get into that a little bit. But before we do that, the reason you -- was the reason you picked the Marine Corps because you had to be at a certain age, and your father could --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Right. Right. And also I always wanted to join the Marine Corps.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I was thinking that that was a great corps to join, and that it was the -- yeah, the epitome, shall we say.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: I was just wondering since you worked with --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: The Air Force.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: With the Air Force, if --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: If that would have -- I mean, the other -- the Marine Corps experience or how you felt about it must have been more significant to you.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: It was.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Than -- than the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yes. Yeah, except for the experiences that I had in the -- in the North Africa.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah. But later on it occurred to me that, number one, I couldn't fly, because if I had gone -- if I had gone in the Air Force, I would have wanted to learn to be a pilot.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Right. Right.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: But I couldn't fly. Apparently I had -- my eyes were not --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: They weren't bad, but they were not what they needed for the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: So just tell me --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: So --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- about anything that you recall from your first days in the Marine Corps, how it felt.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: And your -- you must have had boot camp training, like nowadays?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yeah, prior to that, though, I forgot to mention this, I think Yvonne had mentioned it a few minutes ago, is that when I came back -- I didn't expect this, but when I came back, apparently the fact that an American boy was caught in North Africa.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Oh, thank you.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And things of those things -- I'm sorry if I forgot that originally.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: No, the homecoming?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: The homecoming was very interesting. Not only did I get to know Dorothy Lamour and Joan Blondell and get to dance with them, because I was taken to the American -- to the USO by my friends, et cetera, et cetera. That was very exciting. But it was written up all over the United States in the various newspapers. And that's in that book there, too. And so it was a -- it was a -- it was not only a discovery of a new land, my land, my country, a rediscovery of it, but I was being sort of adulated by the girls, which was great.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Especially at an age of 14.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And the boys -- and the boys were jealous as hell of me. All that kind of stuff. But that's typical of what happens at the time. So that was a lot of fun. So naturally I kept those things and that was part of the -- part of the scrapbook, which will go into the book itself that I'm writing now. Hopefully one day I'll sit down and do it the right way. But now with the computer, you can do an awful lot.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: But I just lost all of my documents the other day because of a storm.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: You didn't have them --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: So I got to recreate it.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: You didn't have them backed up?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I did supposedly have them backed up, but the Dell people didn't do it correctly. But anyhow, that's another story.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I can't cry over split milk, as they say.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay. We have lots of things to cover still. So just tell me just a little bit about, you know, the initial part of your experience in the Marine Corps, before you were sent anywhere.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: The boot camp was very -- it was really an awakening call, shall I say. Because, you know, you went from a -- you went from a totally undisciplined attitude in life towards a completely disciplined attitude, and you learned an awful lot.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: It was very, very hard physically and emotionally. It was an experience that many people could not sustain, and as a result, they got out of the Marine Corps. They were given an early ALMAR to get out because they just could not take boot camp. I mean, they would march you for hours and hours in the midday sun with all of your equipment and everything, and march you through swamps, and have water up to here with all that. So many people drowned. So many people were killed.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Wow you.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: In fact, in boot camp training, I think HB Kaltenborn, who was a renowned American radio announcer.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Where did you --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: He was killed.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Where did you -- where were you in your boot camp?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: PI, Paris Island.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Parris Island is adjacent to South Carolina, and -- well, actually, Parris Island is South Carolina, but it is an island, and it's adjacent to North Carolina and the -- it cuts off the sound maybe. But Parris Island was known for boot camp training.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: You probably know it.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And you probably know about it.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Because she's --

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: My dad was in the Marines so --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. So you know PI, all about PI. And that was an experience, because it is -- it forms -- it forms the mind, and it forms discipline, and so on. But then after a while, you get sick and tired of if, so you revolt.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Do you --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Internally and so forth.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Do you remember any of your instructors from boot camp? Were they as bad as the public or the media makes them out to be?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yes. Oh, yes. Oh, yes. Oh, yes. Oh, yes. Oh, yes. Oh, yes. They were very bad. But, again, later on, and second thought, you say well, I guess, it was done --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Yes?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: -- form a lean, mean fighting machine. That's what the whole purpose of the Marine Corps training was to us.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: And listening to orders?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah. Not only that, but I mean, you know, to make you suffer physically, to make you do things that you wouldn't do normally, or would never have thought of doing, you know. But it was very rough, very rough. It was -- what was it? Eighteen weeks? When your dad went through, it was 18 weeks. He was World War II.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: So it was 18 weeks. So we went through 18 weeks of very hard training. And -- but, again --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: So after boot camp --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: It was an experience.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: After boot camp, where did they send you?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I think -- I think that what happened, I went from boot camp and Parris Island to Camp Lejeune, which is relatively close by. And I was assigned to the first -- first antiaircraft artillery battalion, which is part of the second Marine division. And -- if doesn't matter. The -- I was there for awhile, and then I realized that there was no continuing my education if I didn't take initiative, take the initiative to go into USAFE, which I did, and I finished my high school. Because I hadn't finished high school, and I wanted to finish high school to go to college.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: You were still like 16?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Yeah, okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: So I pushed all that so that I could qualify for college entrance.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And I did all that have on my own. Okay. So that is -- that is what -- that is what happened.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: So when you were at the second place, I won't try to say it.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Camp Lejeune.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Camp Lejeune?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Camp Lejeune.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: What was your assignment there? You were with the battalion, the --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah, first antiaircraft artillery battalion. It had to do with training for antiaircraft, and weaponry and all of that kind of thing.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Did you see combat at that --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Nope. No, no.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Because that was what --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: No, but we were trained for that.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: For it, but you didn't have to go serve --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: But we didn't go. Didn't go.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: That's why -- well -- that's -- that's why I don't qualify for burial at the National Cemetery.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Well, I do qualify, but in a different way. They don't have a -- they don't have the necessary land anymore, or plots, but you can go in there.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Right, it's just --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: You can be cremated and --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Kept there, yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Put to rest in a wall. But I don't plan to do that for a while.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Nope. Good. Tell me a couple of your experiences that you would like to share.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: In the Marine Corps?

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: In the Marine Corps, and how long were you in? Two years? Four years?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: No, no, no. I signed up for two years, and I got out on an early ALMAR so I could go to college.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And what I had -- I had my first year, and I studied --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: You --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: -- to finish high school.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: High school.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And to qualify for college.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And since I was qualified for college, there's no sense staying in since I wasn't going to be a career --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Yeah, no.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: -- person, or an officer.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: You so you were in for a year, year and a half?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah, a year and a half.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Do you have any other experiences you want to share from that particular time?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: One of the interesting things that took place, during my service with the Marine Corps, the French exploded an atomic bomb on Bimini Island, remember that? And there were -- there were a lot of reports in French. And the Marine Corps lent me to the armed -- to the Navy in order to make a translation as best as I could, of course.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Into English of the results of these things. Of course technologically I was nil. It had nothing to do with me. But the actual translation, I was able to handle. But that was a very interesting thing, because, again, I had a command car at my disposal, I had a driver at my disposal.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: And, again, you were very young?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I had the PX -- I had the PX at my disposal. I had the girls at my disposal. That was great. In fact, the driver was a girl. She was a WAC? Was she a WAC?

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Yeah. I think -- forget exactly what it stands for?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: She was a WAC, the women's corps. And she was a cute gal, cute gal, very nice.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: And now you showed me your shirt that had your medals. Tell me a little bit about your -- you had --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Well, again.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- big gold star -- not the gold star, not the gold star?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I had completely -- I had completely forgotten about all of these things, until I got exposed again to the Marine Corps. I was invited -- I was invited to the young Marines birthday party.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And as the oldest Marine in the room, I was the one invited to cut the cake and give a speech. So that was a lot of fun. But these things, the first thing that came in the mail to me was the victory medal. And I said, why am I getting the victory medal? I thought it was the -- the World War II was over, at the end of '45. And they said, no, it was extended into '46, because there were those things that had gotten in when you got in that were still in the -- that had gotten out, and we thought that this was something that would be part of World War II. And while I was in there, I was very interested in all of the -- all of the weaponry and shooting galleries and things like that. So I excelled in -- not in Maggie's drawers. Remember that term? Didn't your dad ever tell you that? Maggie's drawers is when you shot, you got a big white sign on your target that meant you missed completely. I got a few of those. But then I trained and trained and trained and trained, and I got to be an expert -- in a pistol, tar bean, and the -- the rifle. And the others I got, apparently our group qualified for the combat ribbon. I guess it had to do with the Lebanese deal. It was strange how that happened. And then the other one -- there are two others pending now, the good conduct medal, and the presidential unit citation. But that's all I had for that. But again, I still don't know how -- you know how I qualified for it, but they told me I did. So I'm not going to turn it down.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: You -- you did all the things you did when you were in Algeria.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Which was -- that counts.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah, very interesting.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: You may not have been in the official service, but --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- a civilian volunteer.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Someone is looking into the fact that since I was -- since I was not exactly military in the North African campaign, but I was a civil assistant that I qualified to wear the North African campaign ribbons and the things that were awarded to those -- to those people.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh, at that time.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Maybe, eventually I'll take it to my grave, who knows.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Well, before I go on and ask you some particulars about your life in general, having to do with when you were in the service, or prior to that, is there any other thing you would like to share about your experience in the Marine Corps?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Oh, yes, yes, this is an experience that had to do with -- had to do with liberty.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And I was one -- I was one to just take advantage of whatever was in my way. And Camp Lejeune, of course, was very close to Wilmington, North Carolina. And Wilmington, North Carolina, is where they held all the dances. Remember that one? Your dad told you that, too, I'm sure.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: I'm going to have to make him tell me stuff.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: You're going to have to make him tell you stuff.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: We'll have to interview your dad.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And what we would do, of course, we had to get back to base by midnight, otherwise, we were reported as absent without leave. So what I would do, I would -- we would take a special bus back, and at that time, the busses were crowded, because I would wait until the last minute, of course, or I wouldn't have a seat. So what would I do? I crawled up into the baggage compartment, and I slept. And I got away with it several times. But one time I didn't get away with it, because I slept beyond the -- the --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: The place where you needed to get off?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: The gate -- the gate where I was supposed to do it. So he brought me to another gate. I said what the hell, I'll jump the fence, and run in. Trouble is, I forgot completely about the fact that there was a canal between the road and the base. And the canal was quite wide. And I think it was about -- I don't know, 11:00 or something -- 10:30, 11:00. I said, I got an hour to make it. So, okay, I got over the fence and realized the water was there. I said, what am I going to do? I tried to make a raft. It sank. So what I did, and I had heard that in that canal, there were freshwater sharks. There were freshwater sharks, and so that scares -- that scares the hell out of me. I mean, that really -- so what I did, I backed up, took a running jump, ran like a fool, and jumped as far out into the canal as I could, and swam.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: As fast as you could?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And then something went like that to me, you know, I was going to -- I got bumped by something, I said, oh, no, oh, Jesus, and I almost panicked, you know. I almost panicked. And I got to the other side whole and hardy and anxious to run. And I ran and ran and ran and ran, five minutes to midnight, I jumped into bed.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And then guess who came in? The drill instructor came in at midnight. Everybody is here.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: If you had hurt yourself and had some blood --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I could have attracted a few sharks, yeah. Or maybe not, I don't know. It could have been -- maybe it was a turtle. Maybe -- it's your mind is what works. Thank you. Go ahead and push me in. You were talking a while ago you were going to ask me some questions about how I appreciated the gourmet food of the US Marine Corps. Well, in contrast to some of the other services, I think that the one thing that the Marines always did was to make sure that we were very well fed. It wasn't -- you know, it wasn't cordon bleu or anything like that, but it was always very good food. And I really enjoyed it. As a matter of fact, I volunteered to take duty in one of the mess halls myself as a cook, because I realized that if I did that, I could get as many steaks as I wanted, or as many eggs as I wanted compared to the others who were limited. There was always a purpose behind what I did then. So that one --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: You sounded like quite a rascal.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah, I was a rascal. I was a rascal. But I didn't do it illegally, because I worked very hard. And that's where I learned to make my soups. But I made them in vats that were humongous, but I knew how to do the base.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Now, a little while ago you said something about that you got really built up when you were in boot camp. And I was assuming you meant your physique.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Physique, yes, very much so.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: And your weight. So when you went in, do you remember approximately -- you were about 15 -- how much you weighed?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yes, I do remember that. I was a big fatso.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Oh, serious?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Oh, yeah, serious. I was fatso. I was not what I wound up being, I'll tell that you.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: So that did definitely get you fit?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah, and then getting into the Marine Corps, first of all, we had to -- the exercise, callisthenics, so on, you heard about that, I'm sure. And all of these things, and the walking, and the -- the training and all of that, just really trimmed me down. I was -- I was a walking mass of muscle. And I thank God, because I kept that. I was very fortunate to do that. But, you know --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: And you don't think the food -- because of all the exercising that you were doing, that the Marines were having you do, I've always heard that the food is like really fattening and stuff, that they would feed, but it was pretty well rounded so you had --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah, it wasn't your typical Mediterranean pyramid, but that didn't even exist at that time. Or if it did, we didn't even talk about it.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: That's true. Right, right.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: But I know that I was a meat-and-potatoes guy, and vegetable. So I ate a lot, a lot of steak, a lot of vegetables and things like that. I didn't drink, I didn't smoke, so all of those things kept my body in very good shape.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Right, right. So on a different topic -- oh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah. She wants me to tell you about the story about what we would do at night if we were not, you know, in the mess hall and had control of what was going on in the mess hall, we would sneak out at midnight, and we would go to the PX and buy all the ice cream we could, and we would eat the ice cream underneath the barracks. It was against the law. I mean, it was against the rules, you know.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Yeah, you weren't supposed to be out of your room either after midnight.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: We weren't supposed to do that. I would inhale one gallon of ice cream.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Oh, geez. Okay. Well --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: But that was -- that's -- you make your life the way you make it.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: That's right. That's right.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: At least it wasn't booze. It wasn't beer.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: It was great stuff. I love ice cream.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay. We're going to go on to slightly different. How did you stay in touch with your family during the Marine Corps?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Well, in as much as there was no such thing --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: And your mother.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah, there was no such thing as computers at that time, so naturally I kept in touch with the family overseas by letter.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And an occasional telephone call at the right times. And locally, it would just be by telephone. It would be relatively simple. But communication at that time is not what it is today. It's really great today, because you can just get on the computer and discuss things with people, and you get an immediate response and so on. I like that.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: You were only 16, so did you have --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Were you homesick at all? You had been very independent.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: No, I had been very independent. I didn't have those needs. I didn't have that -- yes, I loved being with the family so forth. Had I had a large family, I would have appreciated that, but I had only one sister.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And as a sibling, we weren't very close. So -- but the important thing, is that I would have loved to have brothers and sisters and so. I loved the social interaction of family.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: But when I was away, I was busy. I did things that had to be done, and I didn't think about that.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Unless it was a girlfriend that I was -- I would want to talk to or be with or whatever.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Did you feel any pressure or stress --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- in the Marine Corps?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: No. That never bothered me.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: I don't want to go back there too far.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: But when you were in Algeria and Tunisia --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Did I feel stressed there?

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Did you feel pressure and stress during that time?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I never did feel those things, that I can recall. I don't remember anything of that sort.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Did you do anything special that -- for good luck? Did you feel that you needed anything, like some people carry --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: You mean did I carry a rabbit's foot or something like that? No. Oh, well, I just -- well, of course, I didn't have this at the time, but I had something else. But this is what Yvonne gave me. It's very pretty. It's a --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: It's a Christ head, beautiful. And this is from Mexico, a chain, so I love that. So I wore those kind of things.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Because after all, I was in a Catholic institute, not a convent. You know, an institute for boys, boarding school for boys.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: I am afraid to ask you this, but what did you do when you were on leave? You already told me what you did --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: When I was in the Marine Corps.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: -- when you went to eat, like --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
