sp.p: I loved to go swimming. I loved to go play tennis. I loved to walk. I loved to visit with people and make friends, new friends. I never went to bars, I never smoked. Well, yes, I did, I smoked a pipe. I would smoke a pipe to be smart, that kind of thing.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Sophisticated?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Sophisticated. It's sophisticated, you know.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: So you didn't travel that much when you were in the Marine Corps, just between boot camp and --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: No, but during the latter part of my Marine Corps experience, I chose to take on the responsibility of 150 to 200 criminals. In other words, I was -- I went to USNDB, Portsmouth, New Hampshire. And I was what you call a chaser. I didn't choose the second part of the chaser job, which means that you are given one person, and you are manacled to that person, and you deliver him from USNDB, let's say, to California, that kind of thing. That was rather dangerous. I chose to stay there, and to help the prisoners do what they had to do. And that was -- that was one of the last duties, and that's when I chose an early ALMAR, to get out so I could go back to college, and to really get going in college.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: These were military criminals, or --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah, these were military and some civilians. And there were several people that got killed while I was there, guards, because they treated them so badly. And a couple of days before they were to be discharged, they were thrown in the vats, and they lost their sight, or they lost their puberty, or their whatever. But I was always very nice to the people there. And the top man who was the -- the controller and I played billiards together, and I treated him and everybody else very well. That's why I was given a party when I left, not thrown in the vat.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: But then -- and that was very interesting, because you learn an awful lot about human nature, an awful lot, I tell you.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Now, you have a lot of pictures here.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: These picture types, your fellow service men, or people that you met along -- when you were in the service?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: I didn't do very much of that. I didn't not take that many pictures. Pictures were taken when I was really overseas.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh, okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: But by other people. I was not much of a photographer or -- in a way, that's wrong, because that way you don't have a way to follow your life.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Did you --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: The souvenirs are up here, they are not flashed. It would be interesting if we ever got to a point where technologically we can flash our souvenirs onto a screen. And they say that they are working on things like that now.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: You never know.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Third dimensional. Oh, yeah, it should be very interesting when that happens.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Did you keep a diary?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay. I'm going to ask you a few questions about after you were -- your experiences after Marine Corps.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: You said that you went back to school.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: To University of Georgia. I went to University of Georgia. My brother-in-law had gone there, and I was invited to pledge Pi Kappa Phi, which was his fraternity, which was very nice. And I lived off campus for a while, and then I was invited to visit and to live in the fraternity house. And I spent most of my time there until I went to Europe, when I went to Grenoble to pursue my studies in language, economics, export/import law and things of that kind. And I stayed there for two years.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Was your --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Went skiing, and I went sledding, and again skipping classes to go to Geneva and things like that, what we would do.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: So you were in there for two years, and did that complete your bachelor's degree, until you came back?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: No, it did not. No, it did not. As a matter of fact, I didn't even get credit for it when I came back to the United States --

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: -- by George Washington University, so I had to repeat two years. But while I was repeating two years, I was teaching French.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: And you were at George Washington at that point?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: It was good. Yeah, GW.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Here in DC?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: In Washington DC, uh-huh. No, actually, I was at the University of Maryland first.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: When I came back to start my studies, and then I -- since I wanted to work, I came into town. And so I -- I taught French, I tutored French, and I worked at the cashier's office in the library. So I had two jobs in order to make it.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Well, that's what one of my questions was, your education supported by the GI bill?

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yes, definitely.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Did you develop any close friendships when you were in the service that you --

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: No, except two people with whom I had gone to school with that were in the same area. That's about it. But, again, I guess maybe -- I don't know. It's just -- it's just, as you said before, I was so independent, you don't form close relationships. As Yvonne says, a relationship is a relationship, but a friendship is something much more profound. But you have to have that kind of personality to develop that.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Mine were relationships. And I call relationships friends.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: At the time. But then -- but then again, you would forget them when you leave. If I had put down in a book all the people that I met in my lifetime, my God, I would have a dictionary.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Since -- after the service, or since that time, what -- that was '47 then, '48.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: Okay. '49, 50, '51, I was in Grenoble.

sp.speaker: Mary Mohr
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Peter Marshall Kniskern
sp.p: And then I went to North Africa, and then came back.
